title: Will Shade and Dewey Corley Interview, 1960-05-25

blocks.x: See we're recording today in Tippo Mississippi at the home of Mr. and Mrs. Moe's Allison Sr. and today's date is May the 24th 1960 so let's get your name on here first

Yes your name go ahead Maxine Allison I see and you used to sing this song we wanted? Oh it was my lullaby when Moe's Junior was a baby It was handed down from my husband's father who used to sing it to him as a little boy
Now you'd be drawing that
Well I was drawing already what did you want?
It's your name on here too Oh my name is Moe's Allison Sr.
Merchant and Planet
And I put mine on here Dick Allen And our engineer is Bill Claxton over there he's being solid

Sleep my little baby coon Underneath the big round moon When you're in the tree you're swinging Mammy just can't keep from singing Sleep my little baby coon Hunters like to croon your side Flash of light to find your eyes Don't you weep and don't you cry Just keep still till day goes by Sleep my little baby coon Song The wind's so slow, mmmm, just so
That's nice, we like that. What else did you sing to him?
Sleepytime Gal, this is my answer, terrible. Sleepytime Gal.
You mentioned Melancholy Baby?
Yeah, Melancholy Baby, side by side.
No Brahms lullaby though.
No, no Brahms lullaby, didn't know the words.
Things that were popular around that time. Yes. How old is your boy now? He's 32. 32.

And he got piano playing from his father. He got his piano playing from his father, and his maternal grandfather could play any thing in the world except a piano. Now let's turn it back. It's going, okay.
Do you want to identify? Yeah, I want to identify. Let's see, we're recording today. Yeah, we're recording today in Memphis, Tennessee. What's the address here, man?
225 South 4th Street in the rear.
Uh-huh. And whose place is this?
This is Miss C. Robinson's place.
Oh yeah, but I mean, what's your name in other words?
My name is Will Shade.
And your name? Dewey Colley. I'm Dick Allen. Bill Claxton. Your engineer. And what's today's date, man? I can't remember. May the what?
25th.
May the 25th. Uh, 1960. That's right. Okay. Well, let's see. When were you born, man?
1898, Fairway 5th.
And where were you born?
Memphis.
Uh-huh. And how did you get started in music?
I started from a kid up.
From a kid up, huh?
That's right. Father was a musician.
Oh, what did he play?
He played guitar. He used to make them.
Made his own, huh? Sure.
Ordered the parts. And sears and roll boys in different places. And put them together itself.
Uh-huh.
He was a guitar pick and a shoemaker. What?
I'm going to stop this in a minute.
Yeah, sure.
Now, what did your father play? What kind of numbers did he play?
Oh, blues. Bad house stuff, just like we play now.
Uh-huh. You remember the names of any of them?
Can't tell him. I was too young to know.
Did he die before you got big?
He died. I never seen him before in my life.
Uh-huh. Well, when you got started, did you take any lessons or did you pick up the guitar?
I took lessons from my mother.
Uh-huh. She played too? She played. Where did she play? What kind of numbers? Special numbers. Do you remember the names of any of them?
Come over here, the table is spreading, the rocks of Asia, and so forth like that.
I see. I see. Now, uh, did you ever play with picks?
Very similar to my play with picks, just some time. Uh-huh.
After you got going on guitar, how did you learn how to play the blues?
Well, I was raised up where it wasn't nothing but a red light district and that's all they played, blues and things like that. What neighborhood?
Hunky Thompson, so forth.

What neighborhood was this? That was on Raven Avenue, just between Beale and Lennon on Raven. Used to call it Haddon's Avenue long years back. Used to be a gang of sporting people hanging around there and piano would be running night and day playing all kind of blues, Handys blues, St. Louis blues, Memphis blues, Yellow Dog, all city blues like that was out there, all battle house music.
You remember Benny Frenchy?
Benny Frenchy used to play with Handys.
What instrument did he play?
He played piano.
That's the one I'm talking about.
Yeah, he's dead.
Did he play around the Monarch? He played with the Monarch. Yeah, that's what I'm thinking about. That's right.
He played the Monarch on Beale Street.
What kind of place was that?
That was a crap house. He'd shoot dice, gambling, everything there. Cut, throw, thieves, everything.
Beale Street was a nice, quiet place, huh?
It sure was. In them days, you could see a man dead every morning when you get up out your bed.
What was it like with the policemen? They were nice fellows?
If they could be nice, because they wouldn't lie down there long enough to be nice, they'd run them off of Beale Street.
How'd they run them off?
Throw rotten eggs out of anything, sticks, brooms, umbrellas, anything to get their hands on. Them women down there would look for these wasn't a man.
They had some bad cats down there, huh?
Cats? There wasn't cats. I think it was young baboons.
Well, what did they do, those cats? Did they fight and they'd cut your throat?

They'd go, fight, cut your throat, take your money if you see it with anything. Knock it down if you ain't got nothing, whoop you in it. If you ain't got nothing to whoop you, if you got something, they'll take it. You know, if you get bad on them, rough on them, they'll cut your throat and leave them and throw in the bayou anywhere around. It wasn't them dreams.
Got us anything.
Just leave you laying there, won't nobody know who done done it.
Well, suppose you started walking up Beale Street, what would you see as you walked along?

Oh, you might see most any little thing walking along, cause you don't have to bother nobody to see something, cause you're always gonna see somebody being thrown out of one of them giants or knocked in the head with a baseball bat or brick or something with wings on it or something like that. Anything you might see happen, you don't have to be doing nothing to get you too.
They didn't have any women over there, huh?
Plenty of women, nothing but women. Men all together, cut throat, robbers, thieves.
They had hustling women?
Yeah, hustling women. Cocaine sniffles and needle shooting, hops and all such a junk as that.
What about these hustling women, what kind of clothes did they wear?
Shortest dresses they could wear up to the... Yeah.
Maybe about. Up to the hips.
Up to the hips. Better not to do both. Oh, yeah.
What about the music? Did they have full bands?

Sure, used to hold the band around in the wagon. The county in the wagon, drum, bass, fiddle, everything all in the wagon. WC and we'd play in the Memphis Blues, the St. Louis Blues, Yellow Dog Blues, and all such as that. They wouldn't be out on the street, bailouts and dancing all up on... up and down the street, like that.
Did those bands play with music or not? Would they have the music, sheet music in front of them?
They used to play by music and then again they used to play by ear.
What year did they start playing by ear around here?
Oh, that was around about... around in...
four or five. 1904 and 1905, they were playing by ear then?
Mm-hmm, they started then.
How big a band would they have?
They'd have six and eight feet, sometimes five, just a chord note.
What would they usually have?
Chambon, piano, drums, there wasn't no saxophones in them days. Drums and plankton, banjos and like that. Okay. guitars, violins, so forth.
Did they have a clarinet then? Were they out?
38 clarinet then, they were out. Yeah.
But no saxophones in those days?
No saxophones in them days. The saxophones that came in here a few years back. Oh, that's right.

Okay. Second reel of interview with Will Shade and Dewey Coley. Okay. It's May the 25th, 1960. Thank you. Keep your mic. All right. We were talking about some of the bands they had around here. Do you remember the names of any other ones when you were a little boy?
Oh, W.C. Handy and Howard Yancy, B. Smith. And, uh, oh, quite a few of them. I forgot the name right at the prison. Can't call them right now. So jumped up on me.
How about Howard Yancy? How old was he?
Oh, he was up in the age. He was a man when I was a kid. Knee pants. Oh.
That's the guy right around the corner in the pool room, right? That's right.
He used to have a musician in his headquarters up there. At a club up there. Mm-hmm. I see.
Uh, I see. Uh, now what style of music did you call that that these bands play?

Well, they was playing that ragtime music, you know, and like that, and that Dixieland music down in New Orleans, or like that, way down in New Orleans, all such that. All them old back records that Hannah Beath made, they'd follow behind that, and something else new come out, then they'd read that and pick up on that and learn it, and then they'd play that. Mm-hmm.
I see. Well, now you yourself, did you start out alone, or did you start in with somebody when you started making money?
Well, when I first started making money, I started in with Benny Ramey, Will Welton, myself, and another fella called Roundhouse. But his name was Elijah.
And what all did they do?
One played Jug. Who's that?
Elijah.

He played Jug. Mm-hmm. Ben Ramey played Kazoo. Also, I played guitar. A double, I played harmonica two. Will Welton, he played second guitar. And I played lead. And wrote my own songs. Made up my own tunes. What was that guy's, what was the name of that group? Memphis Jug Band. Mm-hmm. Did you make any records with those fellas? I made that my first record, I made it up to the first record, I made it up to the
first time. And what was the tunes on that record?
Oh, Newport News, Memphis Jug Band Blues, Stanger Woman, Sun Brummers Blues. I only recorded two the first time.
And who else played with the Memphis Jug Band?
There wasn't no one else but that's us the first started out for the last 12 or 15 years.
You changed around a little, huh?
Well, after they died out, I had to get new members and relearn them over.
What about who took Weldon's place? Robert Carter. What did he play?
Dittor.
And who'd you get on the jug?
I had Jab Jones on the jug.
Oh. And did he play anything else?
He played piano.
You say he worked with Sleepy John Estes for a while?

Well, him and them recorded some records a while back. Around about 26 or 27, they made the record called The Diving Duck and The Brickish Jail. Something else they made, but I can't remember what else they made, but I know they made about two or three records.
Where do you think Sleepy John is now?
Brown with Tennessee the last time I heard from him. He done went blind now.
Mm-hmm. When did Charlie Polk come in there?
Charlie Polk, he was the first one who was with me. No, he was the second one who was with me after Roundhouse died. Mm-hmm.
And what did he play?
He played the jug. I learned him how to play the jug.
Well, when did Jab Jones come in? After him or before?
He come in after him.
Mm-hmm.
After Charlie died, then Jab Jones come in.
Yeah. Well, what instrument did he play with Sleepy John? He played the pound and jug. Both, huh?
Yeah.
And who's this fellow Ham Lewis you mentioned?

Well, he come in here off of a show, and he didn't have nowhere to stay, so I let him stay with me. Me and Jab had an argument and broke up, and he got a band of his own. That's the reason he got with Sleepy John Estes. So Ham Lewis could blow the jug, and so I got him. He could blow a little better than Jab. He used to play with the Dixie Jug Blowers in Louisville, Kentucky. Used to be the Dixie Jug Blowers there, and he used to blow with them long years back.
And they're good. I like them.
Yeah, they're good people. Good players.
Lockwood Lewis is good. Yeah. He played that saxophone. He was good with them.
Mm-hmm.
And when did Bozo Nickerson come in?

Bozo Nickerson come in and do it at the same time. They both come from the show together. The show broke up here in Memphis. We went stranded. Bozo Nickerson played piano and sang too. He was a black-faced comedian on stage. Ma'am! He put out Sadie Green.
What did you do at the end of Sadie Green? You told me a while about it. Get on.
out of here too sweet. Had a dog named Too Sweet. It was too sweet to get out of there.
Who were some of the other outstanding musicians around town, either with little blues or jug bands or either with big bands?
Oh, that's Charlie Wilson. He had a pretty good band. Tom Pinkston. He had a good band.
What about Johnny Dunn?
Johnny Dunn had a good band.
What did he play?
He played saxophone, guitar and things, different instruments.
You remember Buster Bailey?
I remember him.
What did he play like when he was down there?
He was all around me. He could pick up most anything he played because he was well acquainted with him.
Have any good washboard players around here?

I had one. His name was Otto Gilmore. He left Winter and caught a raid about eight or ten years ago. I haven't seen him no more since. But I've got one here they call Robert Burris. He played washboard, but he's not as good as Otto Gilmore, but he gets by.
Did Gilmore make any records?
He never did get a chance to make no records with him.
What do you call Robert Burris? What's his nickname?
Robert, that's his name. Wait a minute. Call him Dooley.
Well, who is good kid?
That's Dooley.
Same guy, huh?
Yeah, good kid.
And you said Memphis Minnie was here now, huh?

Memphis Minnie is sick. She got a stroke. She can't talk, can't walk in a wheelchair. Gee, that's terrible. Her husband also is the same way. He got a stroke. Got a stroke way before she did. The first of the winter.
And Frank Stokes and Dan Sane, what happened to them?
They died. Both of them is dead.
And Jim Jackson?
He's dead.
Gee. What did Jim Jackson feature?
Well, he played the Kansas City Blues and some other different blues. I never did keep up with them much.
What did Jim Jackson feature?
Oh, he played the ghetto already. I didn't know he played that.
What about Furry Lewis?
Furry Lewis, he played guitar. Made a record for Wildback. John Hen wrote a vocation. Some other songs he had to play but I didn't know the rest of the titles of them.
Well, I'm glad to hear he's around. I'm sorry we don't have time to look him up.
But maybe
on the next trip.
Well, he ain't so far, man. He's just about five or ten blocks from here. Take a long drive around that city state. You could pick him up anytime. He'd be glad to see you.
We'll catch him on the next trip. Maybe you'll see him in the meantime and can get his address.
How long before you think you'd be back here?
It might be a week. It might be three months. You can't tell.
Sometimes it might be a year.
Yeah, that's right.
I started the devil to fix nine that time waiting on you.
Yeah, well, you better not wait on me. I got too many other things to do.
I got you faded, dude.
Yeah. Well, how much have you been working lately?

Oh, been and fell off here. I ain't been doing nothing much. About once every month, just like you said, about once every month, every three months, sometimes twice a week, sometimes no times every week, just everything and went flop. Yeah, ain't nothing here.
Scuffling, huh?
Just scuffling. Don't lie to do that no more. Police run you off the streets. See what the guitar and thing will run you off.
I think that's what they call public relations.
I'm pretty sure it is. Some kind of relation. I'd like to say some other kind of relation, but I forgot I was talking over the right.
Yeah, go ahead.
Something to your relations. Yeah, I'd like to say the damn nation
all the nation.
I'm going to
need some more. All right, a little more wine. But they won't let you get out there and hustle on the street like with your band.

We used to get out there at this time of day we'd make five or six seven million dollars a piece three or four hours. Three or four hours we could run about seven million dollars a piece four, five, six of us sometimes. But the way it is now if you catch me anything out there you're penal form bound.
Penal form bound?

Yeah, that's the same as the White House. That's a young pen tension. See, they couldn't build that pen tension yet because it didn't have enough water around it so they just built a young pen tension. Penal form, that's what they call it.
What are they singing, the penal forms?
Anything that come in their mind. They get to think about the little, oh, I'm going to see my woman and it won't be long. All the city is that.
They sing while they're working?

Sure, sing while they're working. The captain then they think they're happy they ain't going to run a hole. They're going to be singing, all right, bring me a tune now, old nigga, look like you want to get away with me. Oh, captain, I ain't going nowhere.
Might be heading for the bushes, huh?
You go to the bushes if you get a chance.
You know what Lawyer Green is?
Lawyer Green? Yeah. That's making the bushes. Yeah.
that's what he's worried about, huh? What kind of numbers do they sing while they're working?
Anything coming to mind, ain't got nothing special. Like you sing, you might hear me sing a song, like bottled up and go, tad down, bitch, slash it all, anything.
Oh, how does that whip my woman with a single tree go? Do you remember any of the words to that?
I done forgot so old. I
like that. I never can get any more than that. I have to find the record. If I
have to find the record, you see, I might come back to them. There's so many records I made.
Oh, yeah.
I never forgot the title, almost, songs and everything. It's how the tune I played them in and everything. Playing by air, you can't keep up with your tune.
You don't read it all, huh? I
never read in my life.
Well, that's the best way, probably.
I never read stitch.
Oh, what about Babe Barlow? You want to tell me
about Babe Barlow? She's in Buffalo, New York.
Yeah. And you say you, did you play for her one time?
No, she used to work with us. That's when she did the strip e dance.
What happened?
Oh, everything happened. She come and stripping down and stripping down and see the grass patch.
Oh, my God. So, what did she do? She was rad back, huh?

Oh, she was doing that strippy dance, you know, doing all that hollalula stuff and twisting and going on. when she went back on all forward backwards, stripped down, stripped down, stripped to the last piece. And she didn't know it. She was come to find out all the pieces were all with none of them on there. And they said, do it again, she couldn't find it. There was nothing there to do it with.
Did you ever see this show, Mike and Mike? Never did. Never did. She used to be with them. She was a dancer. What did she sing herself?
I don't know. I never did hear.
You never did hear her sing,
I never did go to shows much and fun of much. I would be busy trying to write up my own song and numbers and things like that.
with. I
made
records with Sun Bremer, Benny Rainey, Boyd Stevenson, and Atlanta Georgia. Who is it? Stevenson, what's his name? Boyd Stevenson. He happened to make the Kansas City
blues in Atlanta Georgia.
And what did he play? Violin. Violin? He
played guitar. And violin too.
He played guitar on the record though. Yeah, I played man.
Yeah,

I see. Played man guitar. And you signed? I made state of Tennessee cocaine habits Avalanche Bob Lee Junior. Oh, yeah. Avalanche man. Avalanche man. Let's get your name down here. We don't have it straight. Jenny May Clayton. Jenny May Clayton. I see. That's the name you recorded on that. Yes, sir. Well, I remembered seeing that somewhere. Where else did the band record, Shade? Chicago, Atlanta,
Georgia, St. Louis, Dallas, Texas. New York. I mean, Atlanta City, New Jersey. Atlantic City, New Jersey, huh? Sure. Ben Barlow, that's where she did the Strip E dance there.
In Atlantic City, huh?

Yeah, playing for the Western House and the Memphis Power and Light and Gas Company in Memphis. The center's there. We had about 5,000 people when the first got there from all across the waters, everywhere, London, England, all over there. We come to find out we had 10,000 to cooperate together. Memphis Power and Light come to Western House. Who
do you think was the best jug player you ever heard? Ham Lewis. Who do you think was the best guitar player you ever heard?
Lonnie Johnson.
Lonnie Johnson, huh?

Sure. In those days, because nowadays he got electric, you see, when he learned to play the guitar, he just playing straight out muscle guitar, making sound like electric guitar dude now. See, they got help now. He didn't have no ! What about piano?
Okay, now what, we're doing a continuation of the interview with Will Shade and Dewey Coley here, May 25th, 1960. What's your nickname?
Son Brummer, S-U-N, B-R-I-M-M-E-R, Brummer.
Now, where'd that come from?
That come from my grandmother.
What was her name?
Annie Brummer.
And why they called your son?
Because she read me and everybody called me son Brummer.
Oh, I see. Okay, well, let's get Dewey now. You can swap places with him, huh? Dewey? Yeah. Let's get your age, you know, when you were born?
18 and 98. Mm-hmm.
Exact age.
February the 18th. Mm-hmm. And where were you born? Halley, Arkansas.
What? Hattie?
Halley.
Halley. Where is that? How far from here?
Oh, about 200 miles or more. Oh,
from a good ways off. That's right. Ever know a guy named Joshua Altheim over there? Played piano, used to play with Washboard Sam a lot?
Oh, I've heard of him, I don't know of him.
I think he's from Altheim, Arkansas.
Well, I've heard of him.
The same name is his. He's a fine piano player.
Uh-huh.
Well, you know who Washboard Sam is? You heard him on records, even if you didn't know him.
Oh, I've heard him on records.
Yeah.

I'll tell you who I do know of. Who's that? Roosevelt Sax. I know him too. I started him off on piano doing call in hell long song. Is that right? I play a little piano myself, not very much blues, but I'm his background, like some room is my background in the drug band.
Oh, I see. You started him off. That's
right.
I'll be.
In hell in Arkansas. His first record record was the 44. I wore my 44 so long until it made my shoulder sore. Yeah.
Did you teach him that?
I didn't teach him how to sing. I just showed him little sketches on the piano as I know. It wasn't very much that I know.
Well, what did you sing out there? What kind of numbers did they have out there in !
Oh, just just ordnett blues that's all just ordnett blues what I should say.
Do you remember the names or the lyrics to any of them?
Well, I don't because I wasn't very much in music at all. See, I don't know songs or nothing like that.
What were you doing at the time? Chopping cotton or something?
Well, I didn't much see no ! I used to work at sawmill and things work on quarter boats and things all
the
time. I never farmed never was farming.
Well, that's good. It's hard work.

That's right. And hard. And hard work too. Yeah. I tell you. And it's too much ups in farming. You got to first wake up. Next thing you if you don't get no money at the end of the fall you be missed. Yeah.
That's right. Yeah. Well, it's too much ups to the work. It's too much ups in farming. Too much down to the prices too.
That's right.
Damn. That's something. Well, let's see. Now, when did you come over here to Memphis?
Oh, I was raised up in Memphis. Been here in Arkansas. I traveled back before. I wouldn't travel before Arkansas and different states like that.
When did you start playing music?
Oh, I started in about 27. 27.
And what instruments did you start on?
Well, St. Blooming started in the blowing jug. I was learning to blow a jug, but always could sing a little blues myself. And I know a little bit about to hit on the piano

It wasn't very much, just some kind of song I'd try to play on piano myself, watch anybody else play, and then I'd get down there and try to play myself, not by no notes or nothing like that, just by air.
Let me ask Son a question. Son, what instruments do you play? We forgot that.
I play guitar, harmonica, jug, and bass, streamlined bass.
What's a streamlined bass?
That's the cane that I play on, one string.
Like a washtub, in other words.
Just like a washtub.
How long you been playing that?
I've been playing that for about 10 or 15 years.
Yeah, well, that's fine. We'll get back to Dewey now. Okay, so you play all those instruments, Dewey, huh?
That's right.
And who were your teachers?
Son Bruma.
He's your teacher? That's my background. And what instruments did he teach you?
Oh, he teached me how to play jug, and I know a little bit about piano myself, see? And I got some little kazooks that I blow myself. He didn't learn me that, though.
You got a kazook with you?
That's right. I blows that.
Can we hear a little bit of it?
I guess you can. You want to hear some of it?
Yeah, just a bit.
Say, son.
Say, son. I know that you use mostly your thumb there.
Well, the reason I lose my thumb, I never play with a pick to do no good. I used to play with my thumb all the time. I get as much out of my thumb as I do a pick. It breaks too many strings.
And you pick with your first finger, too, sometimes, huh?
Sure, I pick with my lead finger on my little lead.
You use your other fingers any?
I don't have to. Then I just have to.
Yeah, well, it sounds fine that way.
Thanks a lot.
Yeah, we all enjoy that.
Thank you.
Okay, well, let's get back to doing now. Who all did you play with?

Well, I played with Charlie Pierce. He played violin. Red Robey. Red Robey played guitar. And the little boy we used to have here, I mean, stuff. He played guitar. All those fellas. And Shaky Head Walter. He played harmonica. Little Walter. Played with Muddy Walter now. We teached him around here. He played his harmonica.
Little Walter.
Little Walter. Right from Memphis. Right from under the jug band. That's us in place. All of them. They ain't got nothing on us.
Where's Muddy Walter from? He's from down in Mississippi, I believe.
He's from down in Mississippi.
Did he play around here any?
He never played around here any.
I see. Who were some of the outstanding people here that you remember? Either jug bands or guitar players or the insta horns or what have you?
Jack Kelly is one of them.
What did he play?

He played guitar. Doc Higgins. They had the South Memphis jug band. He blowed the jug. Great big fella. Called Doc Higgins. And let me see. Two or three other boys played guitar around here. But I just can't remember the name. They played with Jack Kelly. Will Betts. He played violin. And he's dead. Jack Kelly's dead.
You remember Slucks and his Memphis Ramblers?
I don't know of him.
That's a white band around town. I thought you might have heard them.
No, I never know of him.
They used to play the Kansas City Blues and all that kind of stuff too, you know?
Yeah. I've heard of them, but I didn't never remember seeing them.
You remember them, Shane? You say you do, huh?
I remember them well. They copied behind us. We were the first band. Memphis jug band. Ever started a jug band in Memphis, Tennessee. I am.
And Snooks' white band copied after you?
He copied after me.
Pick up on your numbers and all that, huh?
Yes, and Mr. Peer picked up on him.
Oh, yeah.
Yeah.
Well, they made some good records.
I know it.
Well, let's see now. Who else were you thinking about, Dewey? That sounded good. You have any good jug players around? Now, let's see.

Well, let me see. We had another boy. Little jug pretty good around here. Boy called Curly. He died. Other boy used to play with him with a guitar. I called Willie B. He played steel guitar. They were good. I played with them.
What's a steel guitar look like?
Oh, it's a shirt. Shined like his cup. Shined like that cup that girl got there.
I see. Anybody play with a knife around here? A bottleneck at all?
Well, let me see. I don't think no one played with no knife.
Well, Ferry Lewis, he made John Henry with a bottleneck.
That was Shade talking now, huh?
Yes. We were Shade talking. Ferry Lewis made John Henry with a bottleneck.
What did he put it on?
Put it on his little finger.
Oh, yeah. I see now. Put it on his little finger. Did you ever do that? I never did. I've seen them do it. They tune the guitar to a chord and slide it up and down.
I've seen them tune the guitar and Vastapool.
Oh, Vastapool too.

Yeah, cross-noted. And it almost played its own set. All you had to do is just sing. See, I can tune this guitar so now you had to put the finger on up there to record it. Just wrap the guitar like that. It'll sound just like you recording it.
I see.
Then you can tune it in Spanish the same way and do the same way in Spanish.
What's the difference between Vastapool and Spanish?
A whole lot of difference. Quite a difference.
The one is lower than the other?
